answers.answer: Draw the circle on diameter OP; it meets the given circle at the point of tangency, and the tangent length is 12.

steps: A tangent meets the radius at the point of tangency at a right angle, so the point of tangency sees OP as a right angle.
By the inscribed angle theorem, every point seeing OP at a right angle lies on the circle with OP as diameter.
So constructing the circle on diameter OP and intersecting it with the given circle locates the point of tangency exactly.
The right triangle then gives the tangent length: √(13² − 5²) = √144 = 12.

steps: The constant sum of distances is 2a, so a = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 and a² = 25.
The foci are at (±c, 0) with c = 4, so c² = 16.
For an ellipse, b² = a² − c² = 25 − 16 = 9.
With the foci on the x-axis the major axis is horizontal, giving x²/25 + y²/9 = 1.

commonErrors.observed: Placed a² under y² instead of x².
commonErrors.likelyCause: The orientation of the major axis was not read from the foci.
commonErrors.remediation: The larger denominator always sits under the variable matching the axis the foci lie on.

b² = 25 − 9 = 16, giving x²/9 − y²/16 = 1.

commonErrors.observed: Used b² = a² − c², producing a negative value.
commonErrors.likelyCause: The ellipse relationship was applied to a hyperbola.
commonErrors.remediation: Check which of a and c is larger: for a hyperbola the foci lie beyond the vertices, so c > a.

answers.answer: The cone has one third the volume, which Cavalieri’s principle establishes by comparing cross-sections against a reference solid.

steps: Cavalieri's principle states that two solids of the same height have equal volumes if every plane parallel to the base cuts cross-sections of equal area.
The comparison therefore turns on cross-sectional areas at matching heights, not on the outward shape of the solids.
The cone has one third the volume, which Cavalieri’s principle establishes by comparing cross-sections against a reference solid.

referenceExample.prompt: Do an oblique and a right cylinder with the same base and height have equal volume?
steps: Cross-sections match at every height.
Cavalieri gives equal volumes.

commonErrors.observed: Assumed a slanted solid must have a different volume from an upright one.
commonErrors.likelyCause: Volume was judged by appearance rather than by cross-sections.
commonErrors.remediation: Picture the solid as a stack of thin slices; sliding the slices sideways changes shape but not total volume.
